overview.title: 📖 Overview: Liturgy for an Unwritten Holiday
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 24a–24b
overview.hebrewSource: מַהוּ לְהַזְכִּיר שֶׁל חֲנוּכָּה בְּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara first confirms Rav Chisda's ruling: everything disqualified for the Shabbat lamp becomes permitted again for a Festival lamp, except 'burnt oil,' since consecrated items may never be burned on a Festival. That prohibition against burning consecrated items on Yom Tov opens a string of dilemmas about how Chanukah — a rabbinic institution with no Torah source — should be woven into the liturgy: is it mentioned in Grace after Meals, is Rosh Chodesh treated differently there, and is Chanukah mentioned in the additional Musaf prayer at all? A concluding halakha, drawn from Yom Kippur's closing prayer, settles how a day's own character governs which prayers mention it. The daf then turns to a fresh mishna listing which oils may be used for the Shabbat lamp at all.

slides.title: 🔥 Shabbat-Forbidden Oils on a Festival
slides.subtitle: One narrow exception survives
rows: The Shabbat-specific concerns (noise, stoking coals) don't carry over identically
Still forbidden, even on Yom Tov
One may not burn consecrated items on a Festival at all

callout.label: Four independent proofs follow:
callout.text: Chizkiya derives the Yom-Tov burning ban from the doubled 'until morning' in the Paschal-offering verse; Abaye from 'the burnt-offering of Shabbat on its own Shabbat'; Rava from 'it alone shall be done for you'; Rav Ashi from the term shabbaton, itself a positive commandment that a mere positive act (burning) cannot override.

slides.title: 🍽️ Should Chanukah Be Mentioned in Grace After Meals?
slides.subtitle: Rabbinic origin versus the value of publicizing the miracle

nodes.content: ❓ Dilemma: since Chanukah is only rabbinic, do we skip mentioning it in Birkat HaMazon — or mention it anyway for pirsumei nisa?
⚖️ Rav Huna's ruling: one does NOT mention it — but if he wishes to anyway, he adds it in the blessing of Hoda'ah (thanksgiving)
📖 Same question raised for Rosh Chodesh (a Torah-level day): Rav says mention it; Rabbi Chanina says don't
✅ Rav Zerika: follow Rav — supported by Rabbi Oshaya's baraita distinguishing days with a musaf offering (mention required) from days without one (not required)

callout.label: The dividing line:
callout.text: Days with an additional Temple offering — Rosh Chodesh, the intermediate days of a Festival — get mention in Birkat HaMazon; Monday/Thursday fast days and ma'amadot do not, and even skipping the day's mention in the Amida there doesn't require repeating the prayer.

slides.title: 🙏 Chanukah in the Musaf Prayer: A Real Dispute
slides.subtitle: Does a day without its own additional prayer still get mentioned in someone else's?

lines.speaker: Rav Huna & R' Yehuda
lines.text: One does not mention Chanukah in Musaf — Chanukah has no additional-offering prayer of its own, so it has no place there.

lines.speaker: Rav Nachman & R' Yochanan
lines.text: One does mention it — the day itself carries the obligation, regardless of which prayer is being recited.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Compare to Rosh Chodesh on Shabbat: the haftarah reader need not mention Rosh Chodesh, since without Shabbat there'd be no haftarah reading at all that day.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Not comparable — there, the haftarah has no other connection to Rosh Chodesh; here, Chanukah IS mentioned in the evening, morning, and afternoon prayers already.

lines.speaker: Better parallel
lines.text: Rav (via Rav Achadvoi): a Festival's Mincha haftarah reader on Shabbat need not mention the Festival — since without Shabbat, there's no haftarah at Mincha on Yom Tov either.

callout.label: Final halakha (next daf's conclusion):
callout.text: The Gemara ultimately follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle from Yom Kippur: a day obligated in its own set of prayers gets mentioned in all of them, once that day's own character truly requires it.

slides.subtitle: Three positions on lighting the Shabbat lamp

boxes.title: The Sages

Explicitly: sesame, nut, radish, fish, gourd oil, even tar and naphtha

slides.title: 📜 Four Sources for 'No Burning Consecrated Items on Yom Tov'
slides.subtitle: Each Sage roots the same halakha in a different verse

steps.content: 1️⃣ Chizkiya: the doubled phrase 'until morning' in the Paschal offering law (Exodus 12:10) grants a second morning — the Festival's morning is excluded from burning
2️⃣ Abaye: 'the burnt-offering of Shabbat, on its own Shabbat' (Numbers 28:10) — implicitly excludes a weekday offering being brought on Shabbat or Yom Tov
3️⃣ Rava: 'it alone shall be done for you' (Exodus 12:16) — 'it' permits food prep, but not preparatory labors like burning that aren't themselves eating-related
4️⃣ Rav Ashi: the term שַׁבָּתוֹן itself frames Yom Tov as carrying its own positive command to rest, which a mere positive act cannot override

summary.principle: Because Chanukah has no Torah source, the Gemara must work out case by case how deeply it is woven into the liturgy, while the underlying Yom Tov prohibition on burning consecrated items — proven four different ways — explains why burnt oil remains the one exception even on a Festival.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 All Shabbat-forbidden oils return on Yom Tov, except burnt oil — consecrated items may never be burned then
🍽️ Chanukah is not mentioned in Birkat HaMazon by default; Rosh Chodesh's musaf offering earns it a place there

columns.content: 🙏 Musaf mention of Chanukah: a live four-way amoraic dispute
🛢️ New mishna: Rabbi Yishmael bans tar, Sages permit widely, Rabbi Tarfon insists on olive oil

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a day's own essential character — not merely its rabbinic or Torah origin — determines which prayers and blessings must mention it

quiz.q: Which oil remains forbidden for lighting even on a Festival, according to Rav Chisda's ruling as confirmed by the baraita?
o: Olive oil
Sesame oil
Shemen sereifa (burnt oil, from impure teruma)
Naphtha
quiz.e: The baraita confirms that all Shabbat-disqualified oils are permitted on a Festival except burnt oil, since one may not burn consecrated items on a Festival at all.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna's ruling, should Chanukah be mentioned in Grace after Meals, and if mentioned, where?
o: It must always be mentioned, in the first blessing
One does not mention it, but if he does, it goes in the blessing of Hoda'ah (thanksgiving)
It is mentioned only by women
It replaces the entire Grace after Meals
quiz.e: Rav Huna (via Rava and Rav Sechora) ruled that one does not mention Chanukah in Grace after Meals, but if he wishes to, he includes it in the Hoda'ah blessing, paralleling its place in the Amida.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Oshaya's baraita, what distinguishes days that require mention in Grace after Meals from those that don't?
o: Whether the day falls on Shabbat
Whether the day has an additional (musaf) offering in the Temple
Whether the day is a fast day
Whether the day is mentioned in the Torah
quiz.e: Rabbi Oshaya's baraita distinguishes days with a musaf offering (like Rosh Chodesh), which require mention in the Amida and Grace after Meals, from days without one (like Monday/Thursday fasts), which do not.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, why does Rabbi Yishmael forbid lighting the Shabbat lamp with tar (itran)?
o: Because tar is muktzeh
Because of its bad smell, which is a lack of deference to Shabbat
Because tar cannot be lit at all
Because it is too expensive
quiz.e: Rabbi Yishmael's reason, as the Gemara explains, is that tar's unpleasant smell might cause a person to leave the room rather than sit by the Shabbat lamp, which is a lack of proper deference to Shabbat.

quiz.q: Which of the four sages' proofs derives the Yom Tov prohibition on burning consecrated items from the doubled phrase 'until morning' in the Paschal offering law?
o: Abaye
Rava
Chizkiya
Rav Ashi
quiz.e: Chizkiya (and the school of Chizkiya) derived the halakha from the verse's unnecessary repetition of 'until morning,' teaching that a second morning — beyond the Festival day itself — is given for burning the leftover offering.
